extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of human prehistory / archaeology
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter from a popular (general‑audience) history describing Later Palaeolithic and Neolithic humans in Europe, their material culture, art, burial and the archaeological criteria used to distinguish periods and peoples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of Later Palaeolithic 'true men' (Cro-Magnon / Grimaldi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of distinct skeletal types in the Later Palaeolithic — e.g. the Cro‑Magnon race (tall people with very broad faces, prominent noses, large brain-cases) and the Grimaldi race (contrasted type with negroid characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many human traces lack sufficient bones to define type, there may have been intermediate or additional races; in many cases one cannot tell whether particular implements or art belong to Cro‑Magnon, Grimaldi or others. Authorities differ and identification is often uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of migration versus local following of resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish migration in the strict sense from slow seasonal/local movement: true men did not migrate en masse into Europe but followed food and plant ranges as climate ameliorated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect generation‑by‑generation spread tied to changing climate and resource distribution rather than sudden large-scale population replacement; use settlement and faunal evidence to infer movement patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of artistic remains (cave paintings, engravings, statuettes) as cultural indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Cave and cliff paintings, bone/ivory carvings, statuettes and engraved designs are key evidence of Later Palaeolithic culture and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art demonstrates vivid perception and animal representation skill, but should not be over-interpreted as evidence of broad intellectual capacities; variation in artistic quality over time can help sequence deposits. Note also that most imagery depicts animals rather than people and that perspective remains primitive (profile drawing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burial practice as evidence of ritual and social behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Burials often include ornaments, weapons, food and the use of pigments to paint the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From grave goods and use of colour one may infer body‑painting and ritual behaviour; burial contexts supply social and symbolic information beyond mere remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of domestication and Neolithic economy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Neolithic stage is characterized by beginnings of agriculture, use of plants/seeds, domesticated animals (dog, cattle, sheep, goats, pigs), pottery, and proper cooking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of domesticated species, pottery, and evidence for cultivation or storage are central markers of Neolithic life; early Neolithic economies may still rely heavily on hunting and 'snatch crops' before full sedentism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material culture markers for Neolithic identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Neolithic phase is characterized by (1) polished stone implements (notably perforated stone axes), (2) pottery and cooking, (3) domesticated animals, (4) plaiting and weaving, and (5) abundant arrow heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polished tools and perforated axe‑heads, together with ceramics and signs of animal husbandry, are diagnostic; unpolished implements can co-occur, so look at assemblage composition rather than a single artifact type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aurignacian (first Later Palaeolithic subdivision) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterized by very well-made flint implements and a rapid development of art, especially statuettes and wall paintings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign early painted caves and finely made flint tools to Aurignacian contexts; artistic innovation is a hallmark of this subdivision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solutrian (second Later Palaeolithic subdivision) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguished particularly by the quality and beauty of its stone implements; razor‑like unpolished blades as thin and sharp as steel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High‑quality flint blade technology (e.g., very thin, sharp blades) is the key diagnostic for Solutrian assemblages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magdalenian (third Later Palaeolithic subdivision) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterized by smaller stone implements, great quantities of bone harpoons, spearheads, needles, increased fishing evidence, deep reliefs and line engravings on bone; designs on round bones possibly used to print on leather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bone-working and engraved/decorated bone objects, harpoons and signs of fishing activity indicate Magdalenian; fine bone needles (noted as superior) are diagnostic of this period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about patchy and ambiguous archaeological record
rubrics_metrics.description: Archaeological remains are little disconnected patches; it is difficult to distinguish relative ages of deposits and to assign material to particular races or peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect overlapping, mixed sequences; do not assume a single linear progression — several roughly similar histories may be inextricably mixed. Many statements must be qualified and remain tentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of settlement forms (kitchen middens, pile dwellings, megaliths) as cultural evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Different settlement evidence: kitchen middens (coastal refuse heaps), lake pile dwellings (with preserved timbers, nets, garments, and domestic animal remains), and large megalithic constructions (barrows, stone circles) indicate differing social/settlement organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret preservation contexts carefully: lake dwellings preserve organic material and show household organization (sometimes animals sheltered with people), whereas middens reflect coastal subsistence; megaliths reflect large cooperative social/ritual activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool‑material transitions and periodization (Stone → Bronze → Iron) — and alternative period schema
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Stone/Bronze/Iron Ages are convenient but misleading as equal divisions; author argues a truer macro-schema is: Early Palaeolithic, Later Palaeolithic, and the Age of Cultivation (including Neolithic onward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple lines of evidence rather than a simplistic material-based taxonomy; recognize long continuities in everyday life across material transitions (bronze/iron did not immediately transform general life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for horse taming and animal use
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible indicators of taming include cave drawings of horses with marks about the heads suggestive of bridles and a carving showing perhaps a rope; but the horse of the period was a small wild pony, and evidence for riding is doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat pictorial/shallow symbolic indications as suggestive but not conclusive; corroborate with harness artefacts, bone/bit evidence, or changes in herd management to confirm taming/riding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting art and artefact function (e.g., round‑bone designs as printing tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some designs on round bones may have been used to print coloured designs on leather; engraved/round designs may have functional as well as decorative uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider possible practical uses (printing, stamping) for decorative objects; experimental or contextual evidence (wear, residues) should be sought before assigning purely symbolic function.
